analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from relying mainly on algorithms to hire, fire, schedule, or manage workers, and requires human review and disclosure.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2026 by Senator Markey with 6 cosponsors, the bill has sat in the Senate labor committee with no action since its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The No Robot Bosses Act would stop employers with 11 or more workers from relying predominantly on automated systems to make work decisions like hiring, firing, discipline, scheduling, and pay. Workers and applicants could always opt for a human decision-maker, employers would have to explain what data the systems use and how they work, and any adverse action would require 7 days' advance notice. The bill would also create a Fairness and Transparency Office at the Labor Department, give workers and unions the right to sue with statutory damages of $5,000 to $40,000 per violation, and ban forced arbitration and class-action waivers for these claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and job applicants at employers with 11 or more workers — including gig workers and contractors paid for their work, plus federal and state public employees — who would gain a right to a human decision instead of an opaque algorithm for hiring, firing, scheduling, discipline, and productivity monitoring, 7 days' notice before adverse actions, whistleblower protection for refusing to follow a system's output, and the ability to sue in court rather than forced arbitration. Labor unions and worker advocacy organizations gain standing to sue on workers' behalf, seats on four new advisory boards, and a mandatory duty on employers to bargain over workplace AI.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and job applicants facing algorithmic management

how_it_helps.text: Employers could no longer rely predominantly on an automated decision system for any work-related decision, and workers could opt out of being managed by an algorithm in favor of a human manager; applicants could opt out of having their application screened by AI and get human review instead.

Workers would get plain-language disclosures about what data these systems collect, what they measure, and how to appeal their output, plus at least 7 days' notice before an adverse action like firing, demotion, or cut hours — and employers could never use a system in a way that interferes with organizing or other rights under labor and civil rights laws.

Developers and employers would have to run predeployment evaluations and annual impact assessments covering risks to workers' privacy, safety, dignity, wages, and collective bargaining, certify before deployment that the system is unlikely to harm workers' rights, and publish summaries of those reports.

Workers could sue in federal court with statutory damages of $5,000–$20,000 per violation ($10,000–$40,000 for willful or repeated violations), could not be forced into predispute arbitration or to waive class actions for these claims, and would be protected from retaliation for complaining or for refusing to follow a system's output; state attorneys general could also sue.

A new Fairness and Transparency Office in the Labor Department's Wage and Hour Division would investigate complaints, with advisory boards that include labor representatives, funded at $100 million a year for fiscal years 2027 through 2036.

analysis.who_pays: Employers using or selling algorithmic management tools — large employers with 11 or more workers, gig platforms, and the software vendors whose systems they buy — bear the cost of evaluations, disclosures, annual impact assessments, 10-year record retention, per-worker statutory damages, and litigation without forced arbitration. Public agencies and state governments are covered too, and states effectively waive sovereign immunity as a condition of accepting federal financial assistance. Taxpayers fund the new Labor Department office at up to $100 million a year for a decade.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, HR software vendors, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden falls on employers with as few as 11 workers, who must conduct predeployment evaluations, train system operators, provide detailed disclosures, file annual impact assessments, and retain records for 10 years — costs that fall hardest on small and mid-sized firms relative to large ones.

Per-worker statutory damages of $5,000–$20,000 ($10,000–$40,000 willful), state attorney general suits with penalties up to $50,000–$100,000, and the invalidation of predispute arbitration and class-action waivers could drive substantial litigation costs, and courts may presume an entire automated system is one inseparable practice in discrimination cases, making employer defenses harder.

The definition of an automated decision system is broad — any software that produces a prediction, score, ranking, recommendation, or evaluation — so ordinary tools beyond headline AI could be swept in, and the 7-day notice requirement before adverse work actions could slow routine personnel decisions.
It authorizes up to $1 billion in new federal spending over ten years to staff and run the new office.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The worker protections are substantial and target a real, growing practice — automated firing, scheduling, and productivity surveillance — and the notice, opt-out, and appeal rights are the kind of thing workers cannot easily get on their own. The costs are real too: a low 11-employee threshold, broad definitions, and per-worker statutory damages impose compliance and litigation exposure on many employers, and honest supporters would acknowledge the bill was introduced with no Republican support and no chance of narrowing those edges through committee. On balance the bill is designed to shift power from employers to workers, and its main flaw is less its substance than its one-sided path — it was never written to survive negotiation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2026 and referred to the Senate labor committee, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote, and the current Congress ends January 3, 2027.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the bill on June 18, 2026, joined by six original cosponsors — Senators Schatz, Sanders, Baldwin, Warren, Blumenthal, and Fetterman.
The Senate read it twice and referred it the same day to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, which has taken no action since.
With the 119th Congress set to end on January 3, 2027, a bill with no committee action after referral faces the standard fate of most bills: expiring without a vote and needing to be reintroduced.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers using algorithmic management tools and the software vendors that sell them are better off so far, because the disclosure, opt-out, and lawsuit rights the bill would create have not advanced and the current Congress will end before it could.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and workforce-AI vendors, for now

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited six original cosponsors

for.role: Cosponsors (Sens. Schatz, Baldwin, Warren, Blumenthal, Fetterman)

sides.party_line_note: All seven initial sponsors are Democrats or allied independents, with no Republican support on record, and no committee or floor vote has occurred yet to measure a partisan split.

industries.industry: Workforce AI and HR software developers
industries.note: Companies selling hiring, scheduling, and productivity-monitoring systems would face mandatory predeployment evaluations, published reports, safety certifications, a ban on selling for uses outside their stated purpose, and per-worker statutory damages — their core business model of opaque workplace algorithms is what the bill regulates. Their trade secrets could be redacted from public summaries, but the disclosure and liability framework would raise the cost of selling these tools.

industries.industry: Algorithmically managed large employers (gig platforms, warehouse, retail, and staffing chains)
industries.note: These employers could no longer rely predominantly on algorithms for hiring, firing, discipline, scheduling, or pay, would have to give workers a human manager on request and 7 days' notice before adverse actions, and would have to bargain with unions over implementing workplace AI — a direct constraint on management-by-app practices that set schedules, quotas, and terminations with no human in the loop.

industries.industry: Labor unions and worker advocacy organizations
industries.note: Unions gain standing to sue on behalf of workers, guaranteed seats on all four new advisory boards, and an employer duty to bargain over the decision to implement automated systems — new leverage over workplace technology.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican support and a Senate majority and committee chair from the other party, the bill is very unlikely to get a markup or floor vote before the 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027; the realistic path is that it dies at the end of the Congress and would need to be reintroduced in the next one.
